Base directory for this skill: /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/.claude/skills/energy-efficiency

# Energy Efficiency Analysis

You are finding **energy waste**: code that spends energy on work the program
does not need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what
the program does.

**The task is to cover everything you were asked to look at** — every file,
every function and every method — and to report every case you find there, not
a few that turn up early in one or two files. A run that stops after two or
three findings has not done it. Keep going until every file has been read, and
report what you find whether or not it can be measured here.

Why this matters more than speed: a smell in code you never read is never
found. Nothing later in the procedure goes back to code left out of step 1, and
the report then reads as if that code were clean, so a missed inefficiency
costs more than any minutes spent reading. Keep working until all of it is
done — every file read, every suspicion decided, every accepted one given an
outcome. Do not stop partway to report progress or to ask whether to go on;
stop to ask only when you cannot continue without an answer.

Paths below are relative to this file's directory — call it `$SKILL`. Work out
what `$SKILL` is once, at the start, and use it throughout.

**Time:** you have 120 minutes for the whole run, thinking and measuring
included, and the session is stopped at 120. That is enough to be thorough, so
do not rush: give each unit the reading it needs. Run `date` when you start
and again as you go, so you know how much of the 120 minutes is left.

---

## What counts as a finding

> A finding is a **repair**: a concrete edit to *this* code, with a stated
> reason why the edit saves energy. That it does is a separate claim, and only
> a measurement makes it.

Three consequences you have to hold onto:

- **No repair, no finding.** If you cannot write the actual edit for this code,
  you have not found anything — you have recognised a pattern.
- **No measurement, no claim.** A repair is said to save energy only once it
  has been measured. One left unmeasured is still a finding — with no claim
  attached to it.
- **Report the failures too.** A repair you built, measured, and found saves
  nothing is a result. It stays in `submissions.jsonl`, with its verdict.

## One repair, one reason

Attribute each repair to a single reason: the thing about the code that
explains why the edit saves energy.

One unit can have several repairs, and they can overlap: fixing how a function
searches can make a redundant conversion and a needless copy disappear too,
because they only existed to serve the search. The rule is the same either
way — **every accepted suspicion gets its own repair, written against the
original code, and its own measurement.** That is what says what each one is
worth on its own.

- Two suspicions that would get **exactly the same edit** are one repair:
  submit it once, and record the other as `same_repair_as`.
- Two that get **different edits to the same code** are two repairs: submit
  both.
- Do **not** widen a repair to cover a second suspicion, and do not split one
  edit into several submissions to raise the count.

Since each repair is written against the original, at most one per function
can ever be applied. Choosing it is not part of your job: submit every repair,
measured, and the measurements decide.

## How much you may change

The edit should be as small as removing the waste allows. That bounds its
**size**, never its location, and never how much code you may read to decide.

**What must survive is the unit's contract**: the same return value, the same
effect on its arguments and on the module- and class-level values it uses, the
same printed and logged output, the same files, the same exception type. That
is what gets checked, for every repair, and it is the whole of what callers are
entitled to.

Anything **only the unit depends on** is implementation detail: a helper
nothing else calls, state nothing else reads. You may change a helper's
signature, its return shape or its behaviour, if that is what removes the
waste. A list built in `__init__` and searched only in this method is one
repair, made in both. A value shaped wrongly by a producer and compensated for
by its consumers is one repair, made in all of them — when nothing but the unit
reaches them.

Two obligations come with reaching outside the unit:

- **Give every function you change its own entry** in the submission, named
  `path::qualname`, in whichever file it lives.
- **Establish that nothing else depends on what you changed** — no other
  caller of a changed function, no other reader of changed state — and say how
  in `sole_caller_evidence`. Anything else that depends on it is not
  implementation detail: the change reaches it too, and the check on this unit
  would not notice.

What you may not do is bring anything else along. A patch that also renames
variables, tidies an unrelated branch, or fixes a second problem cannot be
attributed to one reason, and the measurement stops meaning anything. The
second problem is a second finding, or it is nothing.

## What is not energy waste

**Style.** Unreadable, undocumented, poorly named, badly typed code is not
energy waste. If the repair does not change what the machine does, it
is out of scope here.

Everything else that wastes work is in scope, wherever it is in the program:
a real repair is a real repair, and the measurement will say what it came to.

## Energy is not time

They usually move together, but not always. Spreading work across cores cuts
wall-clock time while raising energy. A busy-wait poll burns power while making
no progress. A blocked event loop keeps a core hot for nothing. Judge energy,
and when the two diverge, say so — those cases are the most interesting ones
you can find.

## Measuring for yourself

At any step, whenever you are unsure — whether some code costs anything,
whether a change would save energy or only time, whether a version still does
the same work — measure it. `$SKILL/scripts/energy.py` takes one energy reading
of any Python call:

```python
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "...")    # $SKILL/scripts, written out in full
from energy import measure
r = measure(my_function, data)          # r.joules, r.seconds, r.watts, r.result
```

What you run, on what data, how many times and how you compare is up to you;
the script's docstring says what one reading holds. These readings are for
your own judgement, and nothing records them: a repair is still measured by
`verify.py`, in step 3, on the inputs generated for it.

---

## Procedure

Four steps, in order. **Each step writes its own file in the repository's
root, and when the step is finished you say so** — then the next step begins:

| Step | Writes | When it is finished |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Find | `step1.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 1` |
| 2. Decide | `step2.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 2` |
| 3. Repair and measure | `submissions.jsonl`, `step3.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 3` |
| 4. Finish | your final message | — |

Step 1 is breadth: every file read, and every unit where something may be
wasteful put on a list. Steps 2 and 3 are depth, for the units on that list.

While a step is open, its file is yours: write it, rewrite it, fix it. `done`
keeps the file, outside this session, as that step's output, and makes it
read-only — a finished step is never changed. If a later step shows you
something an earlier one missed, say so in the later step's file: step 2
rejects a step-1 suspicion and adds a new one; it does not touch
`step1.jsonl`. Do not start a step's file before the previous step is done.
`inputs.py` and
`verify.py` run between `done 2` and `done 3`.

Every step after the first is a check on what the first wrote down, and a
check you run against nothing checks nothing.

Each record is one JSON line with **exactly the keys its example below shows —
all of them, and no others**; a key with nothing to say is `null` or `[]`.
`$SKILL/reference/output-format.md` lists every key and what it holds. Every
file goes in the repository's root, the directory you were started in —
nowhere else.

### 1. Find — *in:* a target · *out:* every unit where something may be wasteful, with its suspicions

**The target** is what you were asked to look at: the whole repository, a
directory, a file, or a single unit. Choose units only from inside it; read
outside it as far as you need. A unit named loosely — "the render function" —
is yours to pin down: find it, and record the exact `path::qualname` it
resolved to. If more than one function matches, all of them are the target.

Read the repository first — its entry points, what its tests exercise, what
its README says it is for — so that you know what each part of it is for.

**Know what you are looking for:** work the program does not need, work done
more often than necessary, or work done in a more expensive way than its result
requires. Ask of every function whether any of these is happening there.

**Then you must go through every file in the target, and every unit in each
file.** List the target's Python files first, so you know what there is to
read, and work through that list file by file, reading every function and
method in each. Do not stop at the first files that turn something up: the
target is not done until every file in it has been read.

**The list you finish step 1 with is final.** No later step can add a unit to
it, so a file not read here is a file no one examines.

**You may hand the reading to subagents** — on a large target it is the
quickest way to read all of it. If you can start subagents (in Claude Code, the
Agent tool; its read-only `Explore` type fits), split the file list into groups
and start one subagent per group, all in the same turn so they read in
parallel. Tell each to read every function and method in its files in full,
looking for these three kinds of waste, and to report for each its `path::qualname`, its
lines, and what looks wasteful in it. Their reports are leads, not findings:
look at the code of every lead before you list it, and only you write the step
files and run the scripts.

**Leave nothing out because of what you expect later.** Code that calls a
network or a service, code you doubt any input could be generated for, a
script, a long file: read it all the same, and list what looks wasteful in
it. Whether a repair can be measured is step 3's question — ask for its inputs
and let the generator say — and one that cannot is still a finding, recorded
as `blocked` with the message that showed it.

**Record every unit where something may be wasteful**, and in it every
suspicion: the lines, and why. A suspicion is a reason to look closer, not a
verdict — step 2 decides — so write it down whenever you have the reason, and
do not hold one back because you are unsure. Nothing limits how many units or
suspicions you record — one, ten, a hundred or a thousand, whatever the code
holds. A unit where nothing looks wasteful gets no record.

If you were asked for a number of units, list at most that many. You may
change which units those are until you finish step 1; just do not go over the
number.

```jsonc
{"step": 1, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "suspicions": [
  {"label": "a", "lines": [47],
   "why": "`self.buf` is grown with += once per row; nothing reads it in the loop"},
  {"label": "b", "lines": [44,45],
   "why": "`sorted(self.columns)` is recomputed per row and does not depend on the row"}
]}
```

Give each suspicion a `label` — `a`, `b`, `c` — unique within the unit. Steps 2
and 3 refer to it by that label.

Write one record per unit to `step1.jsonl`, and rewrite it as often as you like
while step 1 is open. Before you finish, check the file list: every file on it
has been read, by you or by a subagent. If one has not, step 1 is not finished.
Then run `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 1`.

### 2. Decide — *in:* each unit on the list, with its suspicions · *out:* one record per unit, each suspicion accepted or rejected

Start this step after `step.py done 1`, and write one step-2 record to
`step2.jsonl` for every unit on your list. When every record is written, run
`python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 2`; step 3 starts after it.

**First, read the unit properly.** Read the whole unit, then follow it
outward in both directions:

- **Down, into what it calls.** If the unit calls something you have not read,
  read it. A three-line loop body calling `normalise(row)` may be compiling a
  regex and rebuilding two dicts per iteration, and none of that is visible
  from the loop. Keep going until you reach the standard library or code that
  plainly does no work.
- **Up, into what calls it.** See what it is given and what is done with what
  it returns: waste can sit between a unit and its callers — a result the
  caller throws away, a shape the caller has to undo.

Then say in one sentence what it computes and where its work goes: that is
`what_it_does`.

Read outward because the expensive waste is not in any one line. Some waste
is — a conversion, a lookup, a concatenation — and you can see it where it
sits. The larger kind is in the *arrangement*: a value computed in one place
and thrown away in another; a shape chosen early that every later step has to
compensate for; six functions doing what a different split does in two; a
result recomputed on each of three paths that each look reasonable alone. No
single statement shows any of it.

Read the unit a second time, now with the repair in mind. What the edit would
have to be is usually what tells you whether your first reading was right.

Every suspicion ends this step **accepted** or **rejected**, and nothing is
edited in place. If the second reading changes your mind, reject the suspicion
and add a new one, with a new label, saying what you now think. That keeps what
you first thought on the record, which is the part worth reading later.

A unit's suspicions may also **grow** here: reading a second time to write a
repair is one of the better ways to notice something you missed. Its units do
not — they were settled in step 1. A rejection with a reason is as much a
result as an acceptance.

**For each suspicion:**

1. **Does it apply here?** Does your account of the waste still hold on a second
   reading, or was it the shape of the code rather than what it does?
1. **Can you write the repair for *this* code**, as an edit rather than a
   rewrite of the unit? No repair, no finding.
1. **Does the repair preserve behaviour** on every input, including the edge
   cases and whatever the callers rely on?
1. **State the mechanism** — what work stops happening, and why that costs
   less. "Built-ins are faster" is not a mechanism, and it is wrong often
   enough to matter.

Accept if all of them hold, and give the mechanism as `why`. Otherwise reject,
and give the check that decided it as `why`.

```jsonc
{"step": 2, "unit": "src/router.py::Router.allowed",
 "what_it_does": "checks each request against `self.blocked`, a list built once in __init__",
 "decisions": [
  {
    "label": "a", "lines": [58], "verdict": "rejected",
    "why": "the repair belongs where the container is built, not where it is searched. Added `b` instead."
  },
  {
    "label": "b", "lines": [31], "verdict": "accepted",
    "why": "`self.blocked` is a list searched once per request, built in __init__ at line 31 and read nowhere else; as a set each search is one hash lookup"
  }
]}
```

Every suspicion from step 1 gets a decision under its label, and a unit whose
suspicions are all rejected still gets its record — a run that examined three
functions and one that examined three hundred have to be distinguishable.

### 3. Repair and measure — *in:* every accepted suspicion · *out:* `submissions.jsonl`, measured, and one record per unit

Start this step once every unit has been through step 2, and work from their
step-2 records.

**You do not edit the repository.** You describe each repair; the script
applies it to a copy and reads `before` from the repository as it stands. That
is what makes the baseline something you could not have shaped to suit the
result. Work in a scratch copy of your own if it helps you think, but the
repository you were pointed at stays untouched — and you measure against it,
`--repo .`, never against a copy: a number taken on edited code is discarded.

Read `$SKILL/reference/verifying.md` before your first submission.

1. **Choose what to measure.** Measuring takes under a minute a repair, so at
   most **20** repairs are measured — the ones you expect to save the most
   energy, across all units. Twenty is a limit, not a target: if fewer
   suspicions were accepted, measure those. A place is used only by a repair
   that gets a verdict (`confirmed`, `partial`, `mixed`, `regressed`,
   `negligible`), and it keeps the place even if its line is later deleted or
   edited: once 20 repairs have one, verify.py measures no more. A repair whose
   unit gets no inputs, or that cannot be made to behave identically, uses no
   place, so take the next accepted suspicion instead. Every other accepted
   suspicion is still a finding: record it as `deferred` in step 3's record.

2. **Ask for the inputs of every unit you will measure** — all of them in one
   request. Inputs are asked for here, in step 3: `inputs.py` opens at
   `step.py done 2`.

   ```bash
   python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py request src/render.py::Report.render src/parse.py::tokenize
   ```

   You do not write the inputs a repair is measured on. A generator outside
   this session writes them for each unit: **four** measured inputs that make
   the unit do substantial and different work, and a few edge inputs checked
   only for identical behaviour. It keeps an input only if it runs on the
   original code and gives the same output twice. The request returns at once,
   and generation takes a minute or two, all units together — up to five for a
   hard unit. Each unit's file appears in `.energy-inputs/`, read-only: read it
   to see what your repairs will face. You cannot change the inputs; after the
   session, every repair is measured again on our own copy of them.

   `python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py status` shows which units are ready, and
   for each one that `failed`, why and what to do next. A repair is measured
   by running the original and the repair on the same inputs, here, and
   comparing their output and their energy, so an input counts only if the
   original completes on it from this machine alone and gives the same output
   every time. A unit that needs the network, a remote service, credentials,
   hardware or data the repository does not hold cannot do that, and its
   repairs cannot be measured here. That says nothing against the suspicion:
   it is still a finding, recorded as `blocked` with the reason. When the
   reason is a package missing from this venv, install it and ask for the unit
   again; when the generator simply did not manage, it may on another try
   (three in all). A unit that failed gives its place back: up to 30 units can
   have inputs or be generating at once, failed ones not counted, so ask for
   the next unit you would measure in its place. Up to 30 different units may
   fail in a session.

3. **For each chosen suspicion, write the smallest repair of the original
   code** that removes its waste, as one line in `submissions.jsonl`. Every
   repair is written against the code as it is now, never on top of another —
   so the order does not matter, and nothing you submit changes what the next
   one is written against.
   - **The same edit as one you already wrote** for this unit: do not submit it
     again. Record its outcome in step 3 as `same_repair_as`, with that
     submission's `id` as `submission`.
   - **A different edit to the same code**: submit it as a repair of its own.

4. **Measure the whole file, once.**

   ```bash
   python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py submissions.jsonl --repo .
   ```

   It first waits — up to ten minutes, saying for what — for any inputs still
   being generated, then measures every line in turn, under a minute each, on
   its unit's inputs, and writes the result into that line as soon as it is
   measured, as `agent_measurement`: the verdict in `agent_measurement.status`,
   and the joules and seconds of every input. Never write or edit it yourself.
   Give the command a timeout to match, or run it in the background — and if it
   is still running, wait for it before you finish.

5. **Then fix only what is broken, and run the same command again.** It
   measures only the lines that need it.

   | Result | What you do |
   |---|---|
   | `not_equivalent` | the repair changes behaviour: fix that line |
   | `invalid` | the line is malformed, or the inputs do not load against your repair: fix it as the message says |
   | `no_inputs` | the unit has none: request them if you have not, otherwise record `blocked` with the message |
   | `error` | the environment could not run it: do what the message says — install a missing package here and run again, or record `blocked` |
   | `inconclusive` | the host was too noisy; the next run measures it again |
   | `over_limit` | 20 repairs already have a verdict, so it was not measured: record its suspicion as `deferred` |
   | `confirmed` `partial` `mixed` `regressed` `negligible` | **final.** Do not touch the line |

   A measured result is never revised. Editing a measured line to get a better
   number makes it `invalid`, and the result it had stays on record. If you
   think a genuinely different repair would do better, that is a new line —
   both are kept. A suspicion is `blocked` only when the
   tools showed it cannot be measured: its unit's inputs could not be generated,
   its module does not load, or its repair cannot be made to behave identically
   — quote that message as `why`. One you did not try, because you expect it
   cannot run or it is outside the 20, is `deferred`: ask for its inputs instead
   whenever you can.

6. **Record what happened to every accepted suspicion** in `step3.jsonl`, one
   record per unit:

   ```jsonc
   {"step": 3, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "outcomes": [
     {"label": "a", "outcome": "submitted",      "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
     {"label": "b", "outcome": "same_repair_as", "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
     {"label": "c", "outcome": "blocked",        "submission": null, "why": "inputs.py: no inputs could be generated: every call opens a database connection"},
     {"label": "d", "outcome": "deferred",       "submission": null, "why": "outside the 20 repairs measured"}
   ]}
   ```

Every measured repair stays in `submissions.jsonl`, whatever its verdict —
one you delete is still measured after the session. `partial`, `negligible`,
`regressed` and `mixed` are results, and a file that kept only the wins could
not be told apart from one that hid its losses.

7. **Check, then finish the step.** Every suspicion accepted in step 2 has an
   outcome in `step3.jsonl`, and every line of `submissions.jsonl` carries the
   `agent_measurement` the script wrote, with nothing left `inconclusive` or
   `error` that a run could still settle. Then run
   `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 3`.

### 4. Finish — *in:* the three steps' files · *out:* a short summary

This step writes no file. End with a short summary for whoever asked: for each submission, the unit,
what it repairs, the verdict, and what it saved across its four inputs. Lead
with what was confirmed, say plainly what was not, and say how many accepted
suspicions were deferred unmeasured.

`$SKILL/reference/output-format.md` has the exact shape of every file.

---

## How this goes wrong

Failure modes, in the order they actually happen:

1. **Stopping early.** Reading a few files, picking two or three units from
   them and taking those through to the end. It feels like progress and leaves
   most of the target unread, and the list cannot grow after step 1. Read every
   file first, yourself or through subagents, and pick from all of them.
1. **Repeating what you have read about Python performance.** Much of it is
   out of date, and some of it was never true. Every claim here gets measured,
   and the ones you are most certain about are the ones worth measuring first.
1. **Submitting one edit twice.** One edit is one repair, attributed to
   one reason; another suspicion it also fixes is `same_repair_as`.
1. **Building one repair on top of another.** Every repair is written against
   the original code. One written against your previous repair is measured
   against code that does not exist.
1. **Ignoring context.** Almost every pattern that looks wasteful is the right
   call somewhere. A bare `except` in a retry loop, a materialised list that
   gets indexed twice, a wrapper that is public API.
   Ask what the author was required to do before deciding they were wrong.
1. **Skipping measurement because the waste is obvious.** The obvious ones are
   exactly where a wrong assumption hides.
1. **Rewriting the unit.** A patch that changes everything cannot be attributed
   to one reason, and cannot be measured against one. Change what removes
   the waste and stop.
1. **Changing more than the unit without checking what else depends on it.**
   The check watches the unit's contract, so another caller or another reader
   of the changed state breaks silently.

## Scope

Python. A finding is a repair with a reason, not a label.

A **unit** is a function or a method. That is the granularity at which units are
examined, cleared and reported, and at which a repair is measured — the cases
call something, and this is the something. A function defined inside another
function is not one: nothing can call it on its own, so the function around it
is the unit.

That is all it bounds. Read as far as you need in either direction, and
repair across as many units as the waste requires. When the waste exists
only in the arrangement — two methods of a class that each look
reasonable and are wrong together, a helper whose shape forces the code around
it to compensate — report it against the unit whose behaviour the repair must
preserve, and give every function you change its own entry in the submission.

# Output format

A run leaves four files in the repository's root — the directory you were
started in, next to its README — and nowhere else: not in a subdirectory, not
in a scratch directory. They are your record of the work, not edits to the
code, so writing them there does not touch the repository:

- **`step1.jsonl`**, **`step2.jsonl`**, **`step3.jsonl`** — what each step
  produced, one JSON line per record. Each is finished with
  `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done N`, and read-only after that.
- **`submissions.jsonl`** — the repairs, one per line, written in step 3. The
  script measures each and writes the result into it.

Nothing else is written. Your summary at the end of the run is your final
message, not a file.

---

## step1.jsonl to step3.jsonl

One JSON object per line, in the file of the step that produced it, each
tagged with its step.

**Every record has exactly the keys listed for it — all of them, every time,
and no others.** A key with nothing to say is `null` or `[]`, never left out.
The same keys in every run are what make runs comparable.

| Record | One per | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| step 1, in `step1.jsonl` | unit where something may be wasteful | `step`, `unit`, `suspicions` |
| step 2, in `step2.jsonl` | unit on the step-1 list | `step`, `unit`, `what_it_does`, `decisions` |
| step 3, in `step3.jsonl` | unit with an accepted suspicion | `step`, `unit`, `outcomes` |
| a suspicion, in `suspicions` | | `label`, `lines`, `why` |
| a decision, in `decisions` | | `label`, `lines`, `verdict`, `why` |
| an outcome, in `outcomes` | | `label`, `outcome`, `submission`, `why` |

Step 4 writes no record: its output is your final message.

Shown expanded here; each is written on a single line.

```jsonc
{"step": 1, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "suspicions": [
  {"label": "a", "lines": [47],
   "why": "`self.buf` is grown with += once per row; nothing reads it in the loop"},
  {"label": "b", "lines": [44,45],
   "why": "`sorted(self.columns)` is recomputed per row and does not depend on the row"}
]}
```

```jsonc
{"step": 2, "unit": "src/router.py::Router.allowed",
 "what_it_does": "checks each request against `self.blocked`, a list built once in __init__",
 "decisions": [
  {
    "label": "a", "lines": [58], "verdict": "rejected",
    "why": "the repair belongs where the container is built, not where it is searched. Added `b` instead."
  },
  {
    "label": "b", "lines": [31], "verdict": "accepted",
    "why": "`self.blocked` is a list searched once per request, built in __init__ at line 31 and read nowhere else; as a set each search is one hash lookup"
  }
]}
```

```jsonc
{"step": 3, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "outcomes": [
  {"label": "a", "outcome": "submitted",      "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
  {"label": "b", "outcome": "same_repair_as", "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
  {"label": "c", "outcome": "blocked",        "submission": null, "why": "inputs.py: no inputs could be generated: every call opens a database connection"},
  {"label": "d", "outcome": "deferred",       "submission": null, "why": "outside the 20 repairs measured"}
]}
```

### Field rules

**`label`** names a suspicion within its unit — `a`, `b`, `c` — and is how steps
2 and 3 refer to it. A suspicion added in step 2 gets a label of its own.

**`lines`** is a list of line numbers in the unit's file.

194	# Set on a coding assembled from more than one page. For a flat coding this is permanent:
195	# its merged `display` is in `code` order, not the authored order, so display_order cannot
196	# be recovered. For a hierarchical coding it is transient -- get_codings() clears it once it
197	# rebuilds a real display tree from the coding's fully-merged code -> parent_code edges,
198	# since display_order computed from that tree is exactly as legitimate as a whole coding's.
199	CODING_PAGINATED_KEY = "_dx_paginated"
200	
201	# A backstop against a server bug that returns a `next` cursor that never resolves to null,
202	# which would otherwise hang `-ddd` forever. Far above any realistic dataset's page count.
203	MAX_CODINGS_PAGES = 10000

206	def viz_meta_codings_page(resp: dict, payload: dict) -> dict:
207	    """
208	    Returns a single page of the dataset's codings. Raises rather than exiting, so the
209	    caller can fall back to the descriptor.
210	    """
211	    resource_val = resp["url"] + "/viz-meta/3.0/" + resp["dataset"] + "/codings"
212	    page = dxpy.DXHTTPRequest(resource=resource_val, data=payload, prepend_srv=False)
213	    if "error" in page:
214	        raise DXError(str(page["error"]))
215	    return page

218	def _hierarchy_from_parents(codes_to_parent: dict, all_codes: list) -> list:
219	    """
220	    Rebuilds a nested `display` tree for a hierarchical coding from its complete
221	    code -> parent_code edges, once every fragment of a coding split across pages has been
222	    merged. Siblings are ordered by code, since the wire format carries no other order for
223	    a coding the server had to slice.
224	    """
225	    children_of = collections.OrderedDict()
226	    for code in all_codes:
227	        children_of.setdefault(codes_to_parent.get(code, ""), []).append(code)
228	
229	    def subtree(parent_code):
230	        return [
231	            {code: subtree(code)} if code in children_of else code
232	            for code in children_of.get(parent_code, [])
233	        ]
234	
235	    return subtree("")
236

238	def _finalize_split_codings(codings: dict) -> dict:
239	    """
240	    Turns any coding still carrying `codes_to_parent` back into the canonical shape, now
241	    that every fragment of it has been merged: its edges are a complete parent map, so the
242	    tree hare couldn't safely build from a single page can be built here (see
243	    _hierarchy_from_parents), and the coding is no longer distinguishable from a whole one.
244	    """
245	    for coding in codings.values():
246	        if "codes_to_parent" not in coding:
247	            continue
248	        all_codes = list(coding["codes_to_meanings"])
249	        coding["display"] = _hierarchy_from_parents(
250	            coding.pop("codes_to_parent"), all_codes
251	        )
252	        coding.pop(CODING_PAGINATED_KEY, None)
253	    return codings

256	def get_codings(resp: dict, project_context: str, limit: Optional[int] = None) -> dict:
257	    """
258	    Returns all of the dataset's codings as a dict of coding name to coding, following the
259	    server's pagination cursor and reassembling any coding split across pages.
260	
261	    Each coding has the same shape as a descriptor's `model["codings"]` entry. On the wire, a
262	    hierarchical coding the server had to split sends `codes_to_parent` in place of `display`,
263	    since a tree built from a single page could be wrong; once every fragment is in hand the
264	    edges are complete, so this rebuilds `display` from them before returning -- callers never
265	    see `codes_to_parent`.
266	    """
267	    codings = collections.OrderedDict()
268	    payload = {"project_context": project_context}
269	    if limit is not None:
270	        payload["limit"] = limit
271	
272	    for _ in range(MAX_CODINGS_PAGES):
273	        page = viz_meta_codings_page(resp, payload)
274	        for name, coding in page["results"].items():
275	            if name not in codings:
276	                # Deep-copied so a stored coding never aliases the response, and so every
277	                # key -- not just the ones this function knows to merge -- is safe to keep.
278	                codings[name] = copy.deepcopy(coding)
279	                continue
280	
281	            # Seen already, so the server split this coding across pages. `existing` aliases
282	            # the accumulated coding and is merged into in place.
283	            existing = codings[name]
284	            existing[CODING_PAGINATED_KEY] = True
285	            existing["codes_to_meanings"].update(coding.get("codes_to_meanings") or {})
286	            existing["codes_to_concepts"].update(coding.get("codes_to_concepts") or {})
287	            if "codes_to_parent" in coding:
288	                # A tree built from a single page is wrong, since a code's children can fall
289	                # on the next page; parent edges hold however the pages divide.
290	                existing.setdefault("codes_to_parent", {}).update(
291	                    coding["codes_to_parent"] or {}
292	                )
293	                existing.pop("display", None)
294	            elif "display" in coding and "display" in existing:
295	                existing["display"].extend(coding["display"] or [])
296	
297	        if not page.get("next"):
298	            return _finalize_split_codings(codings)
299	        # Echoed back verbatim as `starting`: when a coding has more codes than `limit`,
300	        # `next` carries that coding's real `after_code` so the next page resumes mid-coding
301	        # at the right code, rather than always just advancing to the next coding name.
302	        payload["starting"] = page["next"]
303	
304	    raise DXError(
305	        "Codings pagination did not complete after {} pages".format(MAX_CODINGS_PAGES)
306	    )

4	class JSONFiltersValidator(object):

6	    A specialized class that parses user input JSON according to a schema to prepare vizserver-compliant compound filters.
7	
8	    See assay_filtering_conditions.py for current schemas, which include optimized schema EXTRACT_ASSAY_EXPRESSION_FILTERING_CONDITIONS_1_1
9	    and non-optimized EXTRACT_ASSAY_EXPRESSION_FILTERING_CONDITIONS_1_1_non_optimized to handle location filters.
10	
11	    Filters must be defined in schema["filtering_conditions"]
12	
13	    There are currently three ways to define filtering_conditions when version is 1.1:
14	    1. Basic use-case: no "properties" are defined. Only "condition", "table_column" and optionally "max_item_limit" are defined.
15	                       In this case, there are no sub-keys for the current key in input_json.
16	                       (see 'sample_id' in 'assay_filtering_conditions.EXTRACT_ASSAY_EXPRESSION_FILTERING_CONDITIONS_1_1')
17	    2. Properties defined as dict of dicts (see 'annotation' and 'expression' in EXTRACT_ASSAY_EXPRESSION_FILTERING_CONDITIONS_1_1)
18	        2.1. If filters_combination_operator is not defined, the assumption is that there is only one sub-key in input_json
19	
20	    3. Complex use-case: Properties defined as list of dicts (more advanced, special use-case with complex conditional logics that needs translation)
21	        Filtering conditions defined this way indicate that input_json may contain more than one item for the current key, and elements are stored in a list.
22	        In this case, the schema must define "items_combination_operator" and "filters_combination_operator".
23	        items_combination_operator: how to combine filters for list items in input_json
24	        filters_combination_operator: how to combine filters within each item
25	        (see 'location' in EXTRACT_ASSAY_EXPRESSION_FILTERING_CONDITIONS_1_1_non_optimized)
26	
27	        Within 'properties' if "key" is defined, then a generic one-key filter is built.
28	        If "keys" is defined, then more complex use-cases are handled via special conditions that are defined in condition_function_mapping.
29	
30	    """

173	    def parse_list_v1(self, current_filters, filter_values, current_properties):

406	    def build_partial_overlap_genobin_filters(

416	                {
417	                    "filters": {
418	                        db_table_column_start: [
419	                            {
420	                                "condition": "between",
421	                                "values": [input_start_value, input_end_value],
422	                            }
423	                        ],
424	                        db_table_column_end: [
425	                            {
426	                                "condition": "between",
427	                                "values": [input_start_value, input_end_value],
428	                            }
429	                        ],
430	                    },
431	                    "logic": "or",
432	                },
433	                {
434	                    "filters": {
435	                        db_table_column_start: [
436	                            {"condition": "less-than", "values": input_start_value}
437	                        ],
438	                        db_table_column_end: [
439	                            {"condition": "greater-than", "values": input_end_value}
440	                        ],
441	                    },
442	                    "logic": "and",
443	                },
444	            ],
445	        }
446	
447	        """
448	        if (
449	            "starting_position" not in filtering_condition["keys"]
450	            or "ending_position" not in filtering_condition["keys"]
451	            or "starting_position" not in input_json_item
452	            or "ending_position" not in input_json_item
453	        ):
454	            self.error_handler(
455	                "Error in location filtering. starting_position and ending_position must be defined in filtering conditions"
456	            )
457	
458	        db_table_column_start = filtering_condition["table_column"]["starting_position"]
459	        db_table_column_end = filtering_condition["table_column"]["ending_position"]
460	
461	        input_start_value = int(input_json_item["starting_position"])
462	        input_end_value = int(input_json_item["ending_position"])
463	
464	        start_filter = self.build_one_key_generic_filter(
465	            db_table_column_start,
466	            "between",
467	            [input_start_value, input_end_value],
468	            return_complete_filter=False,
469	        )
470	        end_filter = self.build_one_key_generic_filter(
471	            db_table_column_end,
472	            "between",
473	            [input_start_value, input_end_value],
474	            return_complete_filter=False,
475	        )
476	        compound_start_filter = self.build_one_key_generic_filter(
477	            db_table_column_start,
478	            "less-than-eq",
479	            input_start_value,
480	            return_complete_filter=False,
481	        )
482	
483	        compound_end_filter = self.build_one_key_generic_filter(
484	            db_table_column_end,
485	            "greater-than-eq",
486	            input_end_value,

488	        )
489	
490	        filter_structure = {
491	            "logic": "or",
492	            "compound": [
493	                {
494	                    "filters": {},
495	                    "logic": "or",
496	                },
497	                {
498	                    "filters": {},
499	                    "logic": "and",
500	                },
501	            ],
502	        }
503	
504	        filter_structure["compound"][0]["filters"].update(start_filter)
505	        filter_structure["compound"][0]["filters"].update(end_filter)
506	        filter_structure["compound"][1]["filters"].update(compound_start_filter)
507	        filter_structure["compound"][1]["filters"].update(compound_end_filter)
508	
509	        # In Python 3, this can be simply done via:
510	
511	        # return {
512	        #     "logic": "or",
513	        #     "compound": [
514	        #         {
515	        #             "filters": {
516	        #                 **start_filter,
517	        #                 **end_filter,
518	        #             },
519	        #             "logic": "or",
520	        #         },
521	        #         {

524	        #                 **compound_end_filter,
525	        #             },
526	        #             "logic": "and",
527	        #         },
528	        #     ],
529	        # }

531	        return filter_structure

5696	Note that all reported data-related values are in base 2 units - i.e. 1 MB = 1024 * 1024 bytes.
5697	
5698	The "interspersed" default mode shows METRICS job log messages interspersed with other jog log messages.
5699	
5700	The "none" mode omits all METRICS messages from "dx watch" output.
5701	
5702	The "top" mode interactively shows the latest METRICS message at the top of the screen and updates it for running jobs instead of showing every METRICS message interspersed with the currently-displayed job log messages. For completed jobs, this mode does not show any metrics. Built-in help describing key bindings is available by pressing "?".
5703	
5704	The "csv" mode outputs the following columns with headers in csv format to stdout:
5705	- timestamp: An integer number representing the number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
5706	- cpuCount: A number of CPUs available on the instance that ran the job.
5707	- cpuUsageUser: The percentage of cpu time spent in user mode on the instance during the metric collection period.
5708	- cpuUsageSystem: The percentage of cpu time spent in system mode on the instance during the metric collection period.
5709	- cpuUsageIowait: The percentage of cpu time spent in waiting for I/O operations to complete on the instance during the metric collection period.
5710	- cpuUsageIdle: The percentage of cpu time spent idle on the instance during the metric collection period.
5711	- memoryUsedBytes: Bytes of memory used (calculated as total - free - buffers - cache - slab_reclaimable + shared_memory).
5712	- memoryTotalBytes: Total memory available on the instance that ran the job.
5713	- diskUsedBytes: Bytes of storage allocated to the AEE that are used by the filesystem.
5714	- diskTotalBytes: Total bytes of disk space available to the job within the AEE.
5715	- networkOutBytes: Total network bytes transferred out from AEE since the job started. Includes "dx upload" bytes.
5716	- networkInBytes: Total network bytes transferred into AEE since the job started. Includes "dx download" bytes.
5717	- diskReadBytes: Total bytes read from the AEE-accessible disks since the job started.
5718	- diskWriteBytes: Total bytes written to the AEE-accessible disks since the job started.
5719	- diskReadOpsCount: Total disk read operation count against AEE-accessible disk since the job started.
5720	- diskWriteOpsCount: Total disk write operation count against AEE-accessible disk since the job started.

41	def wait_for_a_future(futures, print_traceback=False):
42	    """
43	    Return the next future that completes.  If a KeyboardInterrupt is
44	    received, then the entire process is exited immediately.  See
45	    wait_for_all_futures for more notes.
46	    """
47	    while True:
48	        try:
49	            future = next(concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures, timeout=THREAD_TIMEOUT_MAX))
50	            break
51	        except concurrent.futures.TimeoutError:
52	            pass
53	        except KeyboardInterrupt:
54	            if print_traceback:
55	                traceback.print_stack()
56	            else:
57	                print('')
58	            os._exit(os.EX_IOERR)
59	
60	    return future

62	def wait_for_all_futures(futures, print_traceback=False):
63	    """
64	    Wait indefinitely for all futures in the input iterable to complete.
65	    Use a timeout to enable interrupt handling.
66	    Call os._exit() in case of KeyboardInterrupt. Otherwise, the atexit registered handler in concurrent.futures.thread
67	    will run, and issue blocking join() on all worker threads, requiring us to listen to events in worker threads
68	    in order to enable timely exit in response to Ctrl-C.
69	
70	    Note: This still doesn't handle situations where Ctrl-C is pressed elsewhere in the code and there are worker
71	    threads with long-running tasks.
72	
73	    Note: os._exit() doesn't work well with interactive mode (e.g. ipython). This may help:
74	    import __main__ as main; if hasattr(main, '__file__'): os._exit() else: os.exit()
75	    """
76	    try:
77	        while True:
78	            waited_futures = concurrent.futures.wait(futures, timeout=60)
79	            if len(waited_futures.not_done) == 0:
80	                break
81	    except KeyboardInterrupt:
82	        if print_traceback:
83	            traceback.print_stack()
84	        else:
85	            print('')
86	        os._exit(os.EX_IOERR)

89	def response_iterator(request_iterator, thread_pool, max_active_tasks=None, do_first_task_sequentially=True):
90	    """
91	    :param request_iterator:
92	        An iterator producing inputs for consumption by the worker pool.
93	    :type request_iterator: iterator of callable, args, kwargs
94	    :param thread_pool: thread pool to submit the requests to
95	    :type thread_pool: concurrent.futures.thread.ThreadPoolExecutor
96	    :param max_active_tasks:
97	        The maximum number of tasks that may be either running or
98	        waiting for consumption of their result. If not given, defaults
99	        to the number of CPU cores on the machine.
100	    :type max_active_tasks: int
101	    :param do_first_task_sequentially:
102	        If True, executes (and returns the result of) the first request
103	        before submitting any other requests (the subsequent requests
104	        are submitted with *max_active_tasks* parallelism).
105	    :type do_first_task_sequentially: bool
106	
107	    Rate-limited asynchronous multithreaded task runner. Consumes tasks
108	    from *request_iterator*. Yields their results in order, while
109	    allowing up to *max_active_tasks* to run simultaneously. Unlike
110	    concurrent.futures.Executor.map, prevents new tasks from starting
111	    while there are *max_active_tasks* or more unconsumed results.
112	
113	    """
114	    tasks_in_progress = collections.deque()
115	    if max_active_tasks is None:
116	        max_active_tasks = cpu_count()
117	
118	    # The following two functions facilitate GC by not adding extra variables to the enclosing scope.
119	    def submit_task(task_iterator, executor, futures_queue):
120	        retval  = next(task_iterator, None)
121	        if retval is None:
122	            return False
123	        task_callable, task_args, task_kwargs = retval
124	        task_future = executor.submit(task_callable, *task_args, **task_kwargs)
125	        futures_queue.append(task_future)
126	        return True
127	
128	    def next_result(tasks_in_progress):
129	        future = tasks_in_progress.popleft()
130	        try:
131	            result = future.result(timeout=THREAD_TIMEOUT_MAX)
132	        except KeyboardInterrupt:
133	            print('')
134	            os._exit(os.EX_IOERR)
135	        return result
136	
137	    if do_first_task_sequentially:
138	        task_callable, task_args, task_kwargs = next(request_iterator)
139	        yield task_callable(*task_args, **task_kwargs)
140	
141	    for _i in range(max_active_tasks):
142	        retval = submit_task(request_iterator, thread_pool, tasks_in_progress)
143	        if not retval:
144	            break
145	
146	    while len(tasks_in_progress) > 0:
147	        result = next_result(tasks_in_progress)
148	        submit_task(request_iterator, thread_pool, tasks_in_progress)
149	        yield result
150	        del result

160	def normalize_time_input(t, future=False, default_unit='ms'):
161	    """
162	    :param default_unit: units of the input time *t*; must be one of "s" or
163	        "ms". This param is only respected if *t* looks like an int (e.g.
164	        "12345", 12345).
165	    :type default_unit: string
166	
167	    Converts inputs such as:
168	       "2012-05-01"
169	       "-5d"
170	       1352863174
171	       "1352863174"
172	    to milliseconds since epoch. See http://labix.org/python-dateutil and :meth:`normalize_timedelta`.
173	    """
174	    error_msg = 'Error: Expected an int timestamp, a date format (e.g. YYYY-MM-DD), or an int with a single-letter suffix (s=seconds, m=minutes, h=hours, d=days, w=weeks, M=months, y=years; e.g. "-10d" indicates 10 days ago); but got {t}'
175	    if isinstance(t, basestring) and t.isdigit():
176	        t = int(t)
177	
178	    if isinstance(t, basestring):
179	        try:
180	            t = normalize_timedelta(t)
181	        except ValueError:
182	            try:
183	                t = int(time.mktime(dateutil.parser.parse(t).timetuple())*1000)
184	                assert t > 0
185	            except (ValueError, OverflowError, AssertionError):
186	                raise ValueError(error_msg.format(t=t))
187	    elif isinstance(t, numbers.Integral):
188	        units_multipliers = {'ms': 1, 's': 1000}
189	        if default_unit not in units_multipliers:
190	            raise ValueError("Expected default_unit to be one of 's' or 'ms'")
191	        t = t * units_multipliers[default_unit]
192	    else:
193	        raise ValueError(error_msg.format(t=t))
194	    now = int(time.time()*1000)
195	    if t < 0 or (future and t < now):
196	        t += now
197	    return t

199	def normalize_timedelta(timedelta):
200	    """
201	    Given a string like "1w" or "-5d", convert it to an integer in milliseconds.
202	    Integers without a suffix are interpreted as seconds.
203	    Note: not related to the datetime timedelta class.
204	    """
205	    try:
206	        return int(timedelta) * 1000
207	    except ValueError as e:
208	        t, suffix = timedelta[:-1], timedelta[-1:]
209	        suffix_multipliers = {'s': 1000, 'm': 1000*60, 'h': 1000*60*60, 'd': 1000*60*60*24, 'w': 1000*60*60*24*7,
210	                              'M': 1000*60*60*24*30, 'y': 1000*60*60*24*365}
211	        if suffix not in suffix_multipliers:
212	            raise ValueError()
213	        return int(t) * suffix_multipliers[suffix]

38	def _get_types_for_inputs(executable):
39	    exec_desc = executable.describe()
40	    input_spec = []
41	    if ('inputs' in exec_desc and
42	        exec_desc['inputs'] is not None):
43	        # workflow-level inputs were defined for the workflow
44	        input_spec = exec_desc['inputs']
45	    elif ('inputSpec' in exec_desc and
46	          exec_desc['inputSpec'] is not None):
47	        input_spec = exec_desc['inputSpec']
48	    else:
49	        raise Exception("executable {} does not have an input specification".format(executable.get_id()))
50	
51	    input_key_classes={}
52	    for arg_desc in input_spec:
53	        input_key_classes[arg_desc['name']] = arg_desc['class']

57	# val: a value of type string, that needs to be converted
58	# col_class: the class of the executable argument
59	#
60	# return:
61	#   - the value in the correct type
62	#   - any platform files referenced in the type
63	def _type_convert_primitive(val, klass):
64	    retval = None
65	    ref_files = []
66	    if klass == 'string':
67	        retval = val
68	    elif klass == 'int':
69	        retval = int(val)
70	    elif klass == "boolean":
71	        retval = bool(val)
72	    elif klass == 'float':
73	        retval = float(val)
74	    elif klass == 'hash':
75	        retval = json.loads(val)
76	    elif klass == 'file':
77	        if val.startswith("project-"):
78	            val = val.split(":")
79	            retval = dxpy.dxlink(object_id=val[1], project_id=val[0])
80	            ref_files.append(retval)
81	        elif val.startswith("file-"):
82	            retval = dxpy.dxlink(val)
83	            ref_files.append(retval)
84	        else:
85	            raise Exception("Malformed file {}, must start with 'file-' or 'project-'".format(val))
86	    else:
87	        raise Exception("class {} not currently supported".format(klass))
88	    return retval, ref_files

90	# An array type, such as array:file
91	def _type_convert_array(val, klass):
92	    inner_type = klass.split(":")[1]
93	    len_val = len(val)
94	    if (len_val < 2 or
95	        val[0] != '[' or
96	        val[len_val-1] != ']'):
97	        raise Exception("Malformed array {}".format(val))
98	    val_strip_brackets = val[1:(len_val-1)]
99	    retval = []
100	    ref_files = []
101	    elements = [e.strip() for e in val_strip_brackets.split(',')]
102	    for e in elements:
103	        e_with_type,files = _type_convert_primitive(e, inner_type)
104	        retval.append(e_with_type)
105	        ref_files += files
106	    return retval, ref_files

108	def _type_convert(val, klass):
109	    try:
110	        if klass.startswith("array:"):
111	            return _type_convert_array(val, klass)
112	        else:
113	            # A primitive type, like {int, float, file, hash}
114	            return _type_convert_primitive(val, klass)
115	    except Exception:
116	        raise Exception("value={} cannot be converted into class {}".format(val, klass))

118	# For a column that represents files, assume it is named "pair", look for

120	def _search_column_id(col_name, header_line):
121	    for i, col_name2 in enumerate(header_line):
122	        if col_name2 == (col_name + " ID"):
123	            return i
124	    raise Exception("Could not find a column with file IDs for {}".format(col_name))

126	# Parse the TSV file. Create a dictionary with the input arguments for
127	# each invocation. Return an array of dictionaries.

129	# For each line, except the header:
130	#   remove informational columns
131	#   create a dictionary of inputs we can pass to the executable
132	#
133	# Example TSV input:
134	# batch ID, pair1,       pair1 ID, pair2,       pair2 ID
135	# 23,       SRR123_1.gz, file-XXX, SRR223_2.gz, file-YYY
136	#
137	def batch_launch_args(executable, input_json, batch_tsv_file):
138	    header_line = []
139	    lines = []
140	    read_mode = "r"
141	    with open(batch_tsv_file, read_mode) as f:
142	        reader = csv.reader(f, delimiter=str(u'\t'))
143	        header_line = next(reader)
144	        lines = list(reader)
145	
146	    # Get the classes for the executable inputs
147	    input_classes = _get_types_for_inputs(executable)
148	
149	    # which columns to use. Note that a file input uses two columns.
150	    # For example, argument 'pair1' exposes two columns {'pair1, 'pair1 ID'}.
151	    batch_index = None
152	    index_2_column = {}
153	    for i, col_name in enumerate(header_line):
154	        if col_name == BATCH_ID:
155	            batch_index = i
156	        if col_name not in input_classes:
157	            continue
158	        if input_classes[col_name] in ['file', 'array:file']:
159	            idx = _search_column_id(col_name, header_line)
160	            index_2_column[idx] = col_name
161	        else:
162	            index_2_column[i] = col_name
163	    if batch_index is None:
164	        raise Exception("Could not find column {}".format(BATCH_ID))
165	
166	    # A dictionary of inputs. Each column in the TSV file is mapped to a row.
167	    # {
168	    #    "a": [{dnanexus_link: "file-xxxx"}, {dnanexus_link: "file-yyyy"}, ....],
169	    #    "b": [1,null, ...]
170	    # }
171	    columns=defaultdict(list)
172	    all_files=[]
173	    for line in lines:
174	        for i, val in enumerate(line):
175	            if i not in index_2_column:
176	                continue
177	            col_name = index_2_column[i]
178	            klass = input_classes[col_name]
179	            val_w_correct_type, ref_files = _type_convert(val.strip(), klass)
180	            all_files += ref_files
181	            columns[col_name].append(val_w_correct_type)
182	
183	    # Create an array of batch_ids
184	    batch_ids = [line[batch_index].strip() for line in lines]
185	
186	    # call validate
187	    #
188	    # Output: list of dictionaries, each dictionary corresponds to expanded batch call
189	    expanded_args = dxpy.api.applet_validate_batch(executable.get_id(),
190	                                                   { "batchInput": columns,
191	                                                     "commonInput": input_json,
192	                                                     "files": all_files,
193	                                                     "instanceTypes": [] })
194	
195	    ## future proofing
196	    if isinstance(expanded_args, dict):
197	        assert('expandedBatch' in expanded_args)
198	        launch_args = expanded_args['expandedBatch']
199	    else:
200	        launch_args = expanded_args
201	    if len(launch_args) != len(batch_ids):
202	        raise Exception("Mismatch in number of launch_args vs. batch_ids ({} != {})"
203	                        .format(len(launch_args), len(batch_ids)))
204	
205	    return { "launch_args": launch_args,
206	             "batch_ids": batch_ids }

208	#
209	# executable: applet, app, or workflow
210	# launch_args: array of dictionaries, each of which contains all arguments needed to
211	#     invoke the executable.
212	# set_batch_folders: boolean, if True, the results from each batch
213	#     run will be placed in a separate output folder named after batch ID.
214	#     The folders will be created/used relative to the output folder set with
215	#     the --destination arg
216	def batch_run(executable, b_args, run_kwargs, set_batch_folders=False):
217	    run_args = run_kwargs.copy()
218	    exec_name = executable.describe()["name"]
219	    launch_args = b_args["launch_args"]
220	    batch_ids = b_args["batch_ids"]
221	    executions = []
222	    for idx, input_json in enumerate(launch_args):
223	        batch_id = batch_ids[idx]
224	        name = "{}-{}".format(exec_name, batch_id)
225	        properties = {
226	            'batch-id': batch_id,
227	            'batch-name': name
228	        }
229	        run_args['name'] = name
230	        if run_args.get('properties') is not None:
231	            run_args['properties'].update(properties)
232	        else:
233	            run_args['properties'] = properties
234	
235	        if set_batch_folders:
236	            run_args['folder'] = run_kwargs['folder'] + "/" + batch_id
237	
238	        try:
239	            dxexecution = executable.run(input_json, **run_args)
240	            executions.append(dxexecution)
241	        except Exception:
242	            err_exit()
243	    return executions

19	_cache = {}
20	_MAXCACHE = 100
21	
22	def filter(names, pat):
23	    """
24	    A copy of fnmatch.filter that replaces with [^\/] instead of . to match path globs.
25	    """
26	    import os,posixpath
27	    result=[]
28	    pat=os.path.normcase(pat)
29	    if not pat in _cache:
30	        res = translate(pat)
31	        if len(_cache) >= _MAXCACHE:
32	            _cache.clear()
33	        _cache[pat] = re.compile(res)
34	    match=_cache[pat].match
35	    if os.path is posixpath:
36	        # normcase on posix is NOP. Optimize it away from the loop.
37	        for name in names:
38	            if match(name):
39	                result.append(name)
40	    else:
41	        for name in names:
42	            if match(os.path.normcase(name)):
43	                result.append(name)
44	    return result
45	
46	def translate(pat):
47	    """
48	    A copy of fnmatch.translate that replaces with [^\/] instead of . to match path globs.
49	    """
50	
51	    i, n = 0, len(pat)
52	    res = ''
53	    while i < n:
54	        c = pat[i]
55	        i = i+1
56	        if c == '*':
57	            res = res + '[^\/]*'
58	        elif c == '?':
59	            res = res + '[^\/].'
60	        elif c == '[':
61	            j = i
62	            if j < n and pat[j] == '!':
63	                j = j+1
64	            if j < n and pat[j] == ']':
65	                j = j+1
66	            while j < n and pat[j] != ']':
67	                j = j+1
68	            if j >= n:
69	                res = res + '\\['
70	            else:
71	                stuff = pat[i:j].replace('\\','\\\\')
72	                i = j+1
73	                if stuff[0] == '!':
74	                    stuff = '^' + stuff[1:]
75	                elif stuff[0] == '^':
76	                    stuff = '\\' + stuff
77	                res = '%s[%s]' % (res, stuff)
78	        else:
79	            res = res + re.escape(c)
80	    return '(?ms)' + res + '\Z'

17	"""
18	Adapted from http://norvig.com/spell-correct.html.
19	"""
20	
21	from __future__ import print_function, unicode_literals, division, absolute_import
22	
23	import re, collections
24	
25	def _train(features):
26	    model = collections.defaultdict(lambda: 1)
27	    for f in features:
28	        model[f] += 1
29	    return model
30	
31	_alphabet = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
32	
33	def _edits1(word):
34	   splits     = [(word[:i], word[i:]) for i in range(len(word) + 1)]
35	   deletes    = [a + b[1:] for a, b in splits if b]
36	   transposes = [a + b[1] + b[0] + b[2:] for a, b in splits if len(b)>1]
37	   replaces   = [a + c + b[1:] for a, b in splits for c in _alphabet if b]
38	   inserts    = [a + c + b     for a, b in splits for c in _alphabet]
39	   return set(deletes + transposes + replaces + inserts)
40	
41	def _known_edits2(word, NWORDS):
42	    return set(e2 for e1 in _edits1(word) for e2 in _edits1(e1) if e2 in NWORDS)
43	
44	def _known(words, NWORDS):
45	    return set(w for w in words if w in NWORDS)
46	
47	def correct(word, known_words):
48	    """
49	    :param word: Word to correct
50	    :type word: string
51	    :param known_words: List of known words
52	    :type known_words: iterable of strings
53	
54	    Given **word**, suggests a correction from **known_words**. If no reasonably close correction is found, returns
55	    **word**.
56	    """
57	    NWORDS = _train(known_words)
58	    candidates = _known([word], NWORDS) or _known(_edits1(word), NWORDS) or _known_edits2(word, NWORDS) or [word]
59	    return max(candidates, key=NWORDS.get)

122	    buffer_size = min(buffer_size, max_buffer_size)

857	    def _read2(self, length=None, use_compression=None, project=None, **kwargs):
858	        '''
859	        :param length: Maximum number of bytes to be read
860	        :type length: integer
861	        :param project: project to use as context for this download (may affect
862	            which billing account is billed for this download). If specified,
863	            must be a project in which this file exists. If not specified, the
864	            project ID specified in the handler is used for the download, IF it
865	            contains this file. If set to DXFile.NO_PROJECT_HINT, no project ID
866	            is supplied for the download, even if the handler specifies a
867	            project ID.
868	        :type project: str or None
869	        :rtype: string
870	        :raises: :exc:`~dxpy.exceptions.ResourceNotFound` if *project* is supplied
871	           and it does not contain this file
872	
873	        Returns the next *length* bytes, or all the bytes until the end of file
874	        (if no *length* is given or there are fewer than *length* bytes left in
875	        the file).
876	
877	        .. note:: After the first call to read(), the project arg and
878	           passthrough kwargs are not respected while using the same response
879	           iterator (i.e. until next seek).
880	
881	        '''
882	        if self._file_length == None:
883	            desc = self.describe(**kwargs)
884	            if desc["state"] != "closed":
885	                raise DXFileError("Cannot read from file until it is in the closed state")
886	            self._file_length = int(desc["size"])
887	
888	        # If running on a worker, wait for the first file download chunk
889	        # to come back before issuing any more requests. This ensures
890	        # that all subsequent requests can take advantage of caching,
891	        # rather than having all of the first DXFILE_HTTP_THREADS
892	        # requests simultaneously hit a cold cache. Enforce a minimum
893	        # size for this heuristic so we don't incur the overhead for
894	        # tiny files (which wouldn't contribute as much to the load
895	        # anyway).
896	        get_first_chunk_sequentially = (self._file_length > 128 * 1024 and self._pos == 0 and dxpy.JOB_ID)
897	
898	        if self._pos == self._file_length:
899	            return b""
900	
901	        if length == None or length > self._file_length - self._pos:
902	            length = self._file_length - self._pos
903	
904	        buf = self._read_buf
905	        buf_remaining_bytes = dxpy.utils.string_buffer_length(buf) - buf.tell()
906	        if length <= buf_remaining_bytes:
907	            self._pos += length
908	            return buf.read(length)
909	        else:
910	            orig_buf_pos = buf.tell()
911	            orig_file_pos = self._pos
912	            buf.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
913	            self._pos += buf_remaining_bytes
914	            while self._pos < orig_file_pos + length:
915	                remaining_len = orig_file_pos + length - self._pos
916	
917	                if self._response_iterator is None:
918	                    self._request_iterator = self._generate_read_requests(
919	                        start_pos=self._pos, project=project, **kwargs)
920	
921	                content = self._next_response_content(get_first_chunk_sequentially=get_first_chunk_sequentially)
922	
923	                if len(content) < remaining_len:
924	                    buf.write(content)
925	                    self._pos += len(content)
926	                else: # response goes beyond requested length
927	                    buf.write(content[:remaining_len])
928	                    self._pos += remaining_len
929	                    self._read_buf = BytesIO()
930	                    self._read_buf.write(content[remaining_len:])
931	                    self._read_buf.seek(0)
932	            buf.seek(orig_buf_pos)

"""
Adapted from http://norvig.com/spell-correct.html.
"""

from __future__ import print_function, unicode_literals, division, absolute_import

import re, collections

def _train(features):
    model = collections.defaultdict(lambda: 1)
    for f in features:
        model[f] += 1
    return model

_alphabet = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'

def _edits1(word):
   splits     = [(word[:i], word[i:]) for i in range(len(word) + 1)]
   deletes    = [a + b[1:] for a, b in splits if b]
   transposes = [a + b[1] + b[0] + b[2:] for a, b in splits if len(b)>1]
   replaces   = [a + c + b[1:] for a, b in splits for c in _alphabet if b]
   inserts    = [a + c + b     for a, b in splits for c in _alphabet]
   return set(deletes + transposes + replaces + inserts)

def _known_edits2(word, NWORDS):
    return set(e2 for e1 in _edits1(word) for e2 in _edits1(e1) if e2 in NWORDS)

def _known(words, NWORDS):
    return set(w for w in words if w in NWORDS)

def correct(word, known_words):
    """
    :param word: Word to correct
    :type word: string
    :param known_words: List of known words
    :type known_words: iterable of strings

    Given **word**, suggests a correction from **known_words**. If no reasonably close correction is found, returns
    **word**.
    """
    NWORDS = _train(known_words)
    candidates = _known([word], NWORDS) or _known(_edits1(word), NWORDS) or _known_edits2(word, NWORDS) or [word]
    return max(candidates, key=NWORDS.get)

149	def _rel2abs(path, project):
150	    if path.startswith('/') or dxpy.WORKSPACE_ID != project:
151	        abs_path, strip_prefix = path, os.path.dirname(path.rstrip('/'))
152	    else:
153	        wd = dxpy.config.get('DX_CLI_WD', u'/')
154	        abs_path, strip_prefix = os.path.join(wd, path), os.path.dirname(os.path.join(wd, path).rstrip('/'))
155	    if len(abs_path) > 1:
156	        abs_path = abs_path.rstrip('/')
157	    return abs_path, strip_prefix

168	def _download_folders(folders, destdir, args):
169	    try:
170	        show_progress = args.show_progress
171	    except AttributeError:
172	        show_progress = False
173	    for project in folders:
174	        for folder, strip_prefix in folders[project]:
175	            if not args.recursive:
176	                err_exit('Error: "' + folder + '" is a folder but the -r/--recursive option was not given')
177	            assert(folder.startswith(strip_prefix))
178	            folder_destdir = os.path.join(destdir, folder[len(strip_prefix):].lstrip('/'))
179	            try:
180	                dxpy.download_folder(project, folder_destdir, folder=folder, overwrite=args.overwrite,
181	                                     show_progress=show_progress)
182	            except:
183	                err_exit()

186	# Main entry point.
187	def download(args):
188	    folders_to_get, files_to_get, count = collections.defaultdict(list), collections.defaultdict(list), 0
189	    foldernames, filenames = [], []
190	    for path in args.paths:
191	        # Attempt to resolve name. If --all is given or the path looks like a glob, download all matches.
192	        # Otherwise, the resolver will display a picker (or error out if there is no tty to display to).
193	        resolver_kwargs = {'allow_empty_string': False}
194	        if args.all or _is_glob(path):
195	            resolver_kwargs.update({'allow_mult': True, 'all_mult': True})
196	
197	        # include "parts" and a few additional fields in the description so that
198	        # we don't have to call a separate describe method downstream
199	        resolver_kwargs.update({"describe": {"parts": True,
200	                                             "size": True,
201	                                             "drive": True,
202	                                             "md5": True,
203	                                             "checksumType": True
204	                                             }})
205	
206	        project, folderpath, matching_files = try_call(resolve_existing_path, path, **resolver_kwargs)
207	
208	        if matching_files is None:
209	            matching_files = []
210	        elif not isinstance(matching_files, list):
211	            matching_files = [matching_files]
212	
213	        # TODO: this could also be returned as metadata by resolve_path since
214	        # resolve_path knows these things in some circumstances
215	        path_has_explicit_proj = is_project_explicit(path) or is_jbor_str(path)
216	
217	        if is_jbor_str(path):
218	            assert len(matching_files) == 1
219	            project = matching_files[0]["describe"]["project"]
220	        matching_folders = []
221	        # project may be none if path is an ID and there is no project context
222	        if project is not None:
223	            colon_pos = get_first_pos_of_char(":", path)
224	            if colon_pos >= 0:
225	                path = path[colon_pos + 1:]
226	            abs_path, strip_prefix = _rel2abs(path, project)
227	            parent_folder = os.path.dirname(abs_path)
228	            folder_listing = dxpy.list_subfolders(project, parent_folder, recurse=False)
229	            matching_folders = pathmatch.filter(folder_listing, abs_path)
230	            if '/' in matching_folders and len(matching_folders) > 1:
231	                # The list of subfolders is {'/', '/A', '/B'}.
232	                # Remove '/', otherwise we will download everything twice.
233	                matching_folders.remove('/')
234	
235	        if len(matching_files) == 0 and len(matching_folders) == 0:
236	            err_exit(fill('Error: {path} is neither a file nor a folder name'.format(path=path)))
237	
238	        # If the user did not explicitly provide the project, don't pass any
239	        # project parameter to the API call but continue with the download.
240	        if not path_has_explicit_proj:
241	            project = dxpy.DXFile.NO_PROJECT_HINT
242	
243	        # If the user explicitly provided the project and it doesn't contain
244	        # the files, don't allow the download.
245	
246	        # For speed's sake, skip this check (i.e. one API call) if the user
247	        # passed the lightweight argument
248	        #
249	        # If length of matching_files is 0 then we're only downloading folders
250	        # so skip this logic since the files will be verified in the API call.
251	        if not args.lightweight \
252	            and len(matching_files) > 0 \
253	            and path_has_explicit_proj \
254	            and not any(object_exists_in_project(f['describe']['id'], project) for f in matching_files):
255	                err_exit(fill('Error: specified project does not contain specified file object'))
256	
257	        files_to_get[project].extend(matching_files)
258	        folders_to_get[project].extend(((f, strip_prefix) for f in matching_folders))
259	        count += len(matching_files) + len(matching_folders)
260	        filenames.extend(f["describe"]["name"] for f in matching_files)
261	        foldernames.extend(f[len(strip_prefix):].lstrip('/') for f in matching_folders)
262	
263	    if len(filenames) > 0 and len(foldernames) > 0:
264	        name_conflicts = set(filenames) & set(foldernames)
265	        if len(name_conflicts) > 0:
266	            msg = "Error: The following paths are both file and folder names, and " \
267	                  "cannot be downloaded to the same destination: "
268	            msg += ", ".join(sorted(name_conflicts))
269	            err_exit(fill(msg))
270	
271	    if args.output is None:
272	        destdir, dest_filename = os.getcwd(), None
273	    elif count > 1:
274	        if not os.path.exists(args.output):
275	            err_exit(fill("Error: When downloading multiple objects, --output must be an existing directory"))
276	        destdir, dest_filename = args.output, None
277	    elif os.path.isdir(args.output):
278	        destdir, dest_filename = args.output, None
279	    elif args.output.endswith('/'):
280	        err_exit(fill("Error: {path} could not be found".format(path=args.output)))
281	    else:
282	        destdir, dest_filename = os.getcwd(), args.output
283	
284	    _download_folders(folders_to_get, destdir, args)
285	    _download_files(files_to_get, destdir, args, dest_filename=dest_filename)

82	def _construct_jbor(job_id, field_name_and_maybe_index):
83	    '''
84	    :param job_id: Job ID
85	    :type job_id: string
86	    :param field_name_and_maybe_index: Field name, plus possibly ".N" where N is an array index
87	    :type field_name_and_maybe_index: string
88	    :returns: dict of JBOR
89	    '''
90	    link = {"$dnanexus_link": {"job": job_id}}
91	    if '.' in field_name_and_maybe_index:
92	        split_by_dot = field_name_and_maybe_index.rsplit('.', 1)
93	        link["$dnanexus_link"]["field"] = split_by_dot[0]
94	        link["$dnanexus_link"]["index"] = int(split_by_dot[1])
95	    else:
96	        link["$dnanexus_link"]["field"] = field_name_and_maybe_index
97	    return link

1019	def format_currency_from_meta(value, meta):
1020	    """
1021	    Formats currency value into properly decorated currency string based on provided currency metadata.
1022	    Please note that this is very basic solution missing some of the localisation features (such as
1023	    negative symbol position and type.
1024	
1025	    Better option is to use 'locale' module to reflect currency string decorations more accurately.
1026	
1027	    See 'format_currency'
1028	
1029	    :param value:
1030	    :param meta:
1031	    :return:
1032	    """
1033	    prefix = '-' if value < 0 else ''  # .. TODO: some locales position neg symbol elsewhere, missing meta
1034	    prefix += meta['symbol'] if meta['symbolPosition'] == 'left' else ''
1035	    suffix = ' %s' % meta["symbol"] if meta['symbolPosition'] == 'right' else ''
1036	    # .. TODO: take the group and decimal separators from meta into account (US & UK are the same, so far we're safe)
1037	    formatted_value = '{:,.2f}'.format(abs(value))
1038	    return prefix + formatted_value + suffix

1041	def format_currency(value, meta, currency_locale=None):
1042	    """
1043	    Formats currency value into properly decorated currency string based on either locale (preferred)
1044	    or if that is not available then currency metadata. Until locale is provided from the server
1045	    a crude mapping between `currency.dxCode` and a locale string is used instead (eg 0: 'en_US')
1046	
1047	    :param value: amount
1048	    :param meta: server metadata (`currency`)
1049	    :return: formatted currency string
1050	    """
1051	    try:
1052	        if currency_locale is None:
1053	            currency_locale = locale_from_currency_code(meta['dxCode'])
1054	        if currency_locale is None:
1055	            return format_currency_from_meta(value, meta)
1056	        else:
1057	            locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, currency_locale)
1058	            return locale.currency(value, grouping=True)
1059	    except locale.Error:
1060	        # .. locale is probably not available -> fallback to format manually
1061	        return format_currency_from_meta(value, meta)

2010	    Attributes
2011	        data - dictionary of entity name to pandas dataframe representing entity with fields, relationships, etc.

2016	    def __init__(self, descriptor, codings=None):
2017	        self.data_dictionary = self.load_data_dictionary(descriptor)
