## Changing more than the unit

The unit's **contract** is what has to survive: everything a caller can see,
listed under "What "the same" means" below.
Anything only the unit depends on — a helper nothing else calls, state nothing
else reads — is implementation detail, and may change.

Give each changed function its own entry in `changed`, in whatever file it
lives, and fill in `sole_caller_evidence`: the search you ran, or the call sites
and attribute reads you checked. The check watches the unit's contract only, so
anything else broken by the change would pass every check here. A submission
that changes more than the unit without this is rejected.

## Several repairs in one unit

Each repair is written against the original code and measured against it, on
its own. There is no order to take them in, and no repair is built on another.

- **The same edit** for two suspicions is one repair. Submit it once; the other
one reason and the result is unusable.

- **Different edits to the same code** are separate repairs. Submit each.

  savings are measured on identical inputs and can be compared.

## The inputs

You do not write them. Ask for every unit you will measure, in one request:

```bash

```

A generator outside this session writes each unit's inputs from the
repository's own code — the unit, its class, what it uses, and where the
repository calls it. It asks for more candidates than it needs, runs each on
the original code, keeps those that complete and give the same output on a
second, fresh run, and of those keeps the four that do the most work. They are
fixed for the unit: every repair of it is measured on the same four, and so is
the re-measurement after the session, which uses our own copy of them.

inputs or be generating at once: more than the 20 repairs measured, so there is
room for units you decide against. A unit that fails gives its place back, so
ask for another in its place; up to 30 different units may fail in a session.

verify.py does not measure while anything is still being generated: it waits
first, up to ten minutes, printing which units it is waiting for. Give its
first run a timeout to match — fifteen minutes plus a minute per repair — or
run it in the background. A unit still not ready after that comes back
`no_inputs` and is measured by the next run.

**A module that does work when it is imported can still be measured** — a
script that reads `sys.argv`, opens files or calls a server at its top level.
When importing it fails, it is loaded one top-level statement at a time: the
statements that fail are skipped and reported, and the unit is measured if it
is still defined. So ask for its inputs rather than assuming it cannot run; the
generator says so when it cannot.

**A unit listed as `failed` can be asked for again** once you have fixed what
stopped it. If the reason is a package missing from this environment, install
it into this venv — whatever you install stays for the re-measurement after
the session — and request the unit again; it is generated once more, up to
three times a session. When the generator simply did not manage — none of its
inputs ran on the original, or it produced none — another try may succeed: it

Each unit's inputs are one file in `.energy-inputs/`, read-only. Read it before
you write the repair: it is exactly what the repair will be measured on. They
cannot be changed, and editing the file would change nothing that counts —
the result after the session is measured on our copy.
The file defines two functions, each returning `(label, thunk)` pairs:

  versions run them and must behave the same; they are never measured.

  work. Every one counts on its own: a repair is `confirmed` only if it saves

takes keyword arguments. **A method takes its instance as the first
argument**, so the thunk builds the instance and passes it.

energy meter to see, so each input is called many times in a row and the
energy of all the calls is added up. That is the only reason for the
repetition. Every call gets a fresh copy of the input, built before the
calls are measured, and the outputs are compared once, before anything is
measured.

completion on an event loop of its own, and a generator's output is collected

generator counts as returning something different.

`WORKDIR`, a directory the script gives each side, and every file the unit
creates, changes or deletes, under `WORKDIR` or inside the repository, has to
come out the same on both sides.

content.text:
The run is complete, but only part of it is measured. I read all 152 Python files, listed 57 units and accepted 55 suspicions. Of those 55, 21 were measured, 15 were blocked by the measurement tools, and 18 were deferred. I changed nothing in the repository, and the record files sit in the repo root. They are `step1.jsonl`, `step2.jsonl`, `step3.jsonl` and `submissions.jsonl`.

Six subagents did the first reading of the files. Their reports were leads, and I looked at the code for the repairs I submitted. I did not independently re-read the leads that stayed deferred.

The energy figures are savings on the generated inputs for each function, not on a whole `dx` command. `dx` spends most of its time waiting on the network, so these savings will be small there.

The command was `python .claude/skills/energy-efficiency/scripts/verify.py submissions.jsonl --repo .`. The seed is whatever the generator fixed for each input set, which I did not control. The noise floor was ±1.7%.

**Confirmed (energy saved on all four inputs)**

| Unit | Edit | Saving per input |
|---|---|---|
| `fp-validate`: `filter_to_payload.py::validate_JSON` | drop a schema-file read whose result is never used | 100% on all four |
| `dxlog-bsearch`: `dxlog.py::DXLogHandler.truncate_message` | bisect the cut point instead of trimming one byte per pass | 99.6–99.9% |
| `resolver-first-pos`: `resolver.py::get_first_pos_of_char` | forward scan that stops at the first unescaped hit | 54–100% |
| `pp-flatten`: `pretty_print.py::flatten_json_array` | one regex pass instead of one rescan per joined line | 85–97% |
| `resolver-last-pos`: `resolver.py::get_last_pos_of_char` | `rfind` with an end bound instead of a slice copy | 35–84% |
| `cohort-pheno-reduce`: `cohort_filter_payload.py::generate_pheno_filter` | linear id conversion instead of quadratic `reduce(a+[x])` | 19–84% |
| `resolver-split`: `resolver.py::split_unescaped` | inline scan, no per-piece slice | 45–77% |
| `nb-insert`: `nextflow_builder.py::prepare_custom_inputs` | collect required inputs and reverse once instead of `insert(0)` | 13–36% |
| `gu-infer-hoist`: `germline_utils.py::infer_genotype_type` | bind the per-locus lookups once | 8–14% |
| `nt-concat`: `nextflow_templates.py::get_nextflow_src` | list join instead of `+=` per input | 6–10% |

**Partial or mixed**
- `sr-cluster-copy` (`override_cluster_spec`, filter before deep copy) saved 99.8% on one input and nothing on the other three.
- `resolver-dxlink` (`_maybe_convert_stringified_dxlink`, skip the JSON parse for paths that cannot be dicts) saved 100% on one input and was flat or slightly worse on three.
- `nb-required-set` (a set for the `required` list in `prepare_custom_inputs`) saved 6.5% on one input and lost 2% on another.

**Negligible**
- `dd-coding-index` (position dict in `create_coding_name_dframe`) and `pp-escape` (fast path in `escape_unicode_string`) both moved less than the noise.

**Regressed or invalid**
- `search-limit` (`_find`, stop paging after `limit`) cost about 21–23% more energy.
- `gu-harmonize-results` (dict comprehension in `harmonize_germline_results`) cost 5–16% more.
- `describe-locale` (`format_currency`, skip `setlocale`) cost 29–37% more, because the extra query call costs more than the call it avoids.
- `pp-table-len` (`format_table`, read the first row without copying the table) cost about 2% more.
- `spell-edits2` (`_known_edits2`) cost 48 to 153 times more energy. The generated inputs use dictionaries of 15,000 to 80,000 words, while `dx` only passes about 100 command names. The edit may well win at that size, but I did not measure it there.
- `dxlog-encode` (`truncate_message`, move the `encode` below the early return) was `not_equivalent`. The original raises `AttributeError` on a `None` message and the edit returns `None`.

**Not measured**
- `oh-sets` (`write_expression_output`) and `dd-load-assign` (`load_data_dictionary`) got `no_inputs`, because the generator failed on both.
- `resolver-colon` (`resolve_path`) was `over_limit`, since 20 repairs already had a verdict.
- 15 suspicions are `blocked` because their units need the DNAnexus API, and the generator said no input can run them offline. They include:
  - the descriptor re-downloads in `extract_assay_expression`
  - the `dx cat` manifest download in `retrieve_bins`
  - the `DXFile._write2` quadratic slicing
  - `find_executions`
  - the polling and redundant `describe` calls in `cd`, `get_valid_bill_to` and `_assert_executable_regions_match`
- 18 suspicions are `deferred` without a repair. Most are network units (`ssh` polling, `archive`, `run_body`, `watch`, `get_database`, `DXDatabase.get_download_url`, the unused hash in `_download_dxdatabasefile`). Four were never requested because the generator was already holding 30 units.

I rejected two candidates on the second reading. The `md5_hasher` fallback does not apply on Python 3.9 and later, and the `DXConfig.get_session_conf_dir` cleanup is an effect callers rely on.
